title: Computer Organization and Architecture DPP Questions

questions.title: Fetch Cycle Sequence
questions.question: The sequence of events that happens during a typical fetch operation is:
questions.solution: The PC address is copied to MAR, memory is read into MDR, and MDR is then copied to IR: PC → MAR → Memory → MDR → IR.

questions.title: Load to AC Micro-operations
questions.question: Which set of instructions transfers the memory word specified by the effective address to AC (Load to AC)?
options: DR ← [MAR], AC ← AC + DR, E ← Cout, SC ← 0
questions.solution: LDA reads the memory word into DR, copies DR to AC and clears SC. Option (c) is STA and option (d) is ADD.

questions.title: Horizontal Control Word Size
questions.question: Consider a CPU with 128 instructions, where each operation needs 8 cycles. 60 control signals must be generated by the control unit. If the signal address field format is used, what is the minimum size of the control word with horizontal micro-programming?
questions.solution: Horizontal: one bit per control signal = 60 bits. Control memory holds 128 × 8 = 1024 micro-instructions, so the address field needs log2(1024) = 10 bits. Control word = 60 + 10 = 70 bits.

questions.title: Address Bits in Control Word
questions.question: Consider a single address field format used for branch control logic. The control word is 64 bits wide. The control portion of the micro-instruction is divided into two fields: a micro-operation field of 24 bits, and an address selection field that specifies a condition based on the flags that causes a micro-instruction branch. There are 16 flags. How many bits are there in the address field?
questions.solution: Address selection field = log2(16) = 4 bits. Address field = 64 − 24 − 4 = 36 bits.

questions.title: False Statement about CISC
questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about CISC architecture?
options: CISC machine instructions may include complex addressing modes, which require many clock cycles to carry out.
CISC control units are typically micro-programmed, allowing the instruction set to be more flexible.
In the CISC instruction set, all arithmetic/logic instructions must be register based.
questions.solution: Requiring all arithmetic/logic instructions to be register based is a RISC (load/store) feature, not CISC. CISC allows memory operands in ALU instructions.

questions.title: Indirect Operand Fetch Micro-program
questions.question: Which of the following is the micro-program of the indirect operand fetch cycle?
options: t1: MAR ← IR[Address], t2: MBR ← Memory[MAR], t3: AC ← MBR
t1: MAR ← (PC), t2: MBR ← Memory, PC ← (PC) + 1, t3: IR ← MBR
t1: MAR ← (IR[Address]), t2: MBR ← Memory, t3: MAR ← MBR, t4: MBR ← Memory, t5: Accumulator ← MBR
questions.solution: Indirect addressing needs two memory reads: first to get the effective address (t1–t2, then t3: MAR ← MBR), then to get the operand (t4), and finally the operand is moved to the accumulator (t5). Option (a) is direct, option (b) is the instruction fetch.

questions.title: Cycles for Indirect Operand Fetch
questions.question: For operand fetch using indirect addressing mode, how many memory cycles are required to bring the operand into the CPU?
questions.solution: One memory access to fetch the effective address (pointer) and one more to fetch the operand: 2 memory cycles.

questions.title: Horizontal vs Vertical Control Bits
questions.question: Consider a micro-programmed control unit design which supports 7 groups of mutually exclusive control signals: Gr1 (2 signals), Gr2 (10), Gr3 (4), Gr4 (1), Gr5 (18), Gr6 (23), Gr7 (6). How many more control bits are required using horizontal micro-programming over vertical micro-programming?
questions.solution: Horizontal = 2+10+4+1+18+23+6 = 64 bits. Vertical (encoded, with one code for no-operation) = ⌈log2(n+1)⌉ per group = 2+4+3+1+5+5+3 = 23 bits. Difference = 64 − 23 = 41. (If no no-op code is assumed, vertical = 20 bits and the difference is 44.)

questions.title: Control Signals at a Time
questions.question: Consider a hypothetical control unit which supports 512 bytes of control word memory. If the control word is 20 bits long and the hardware contains 4 flags and supports 16 branch conditions, what is the maximum number of control signals that can be generated at a time using horizontal and vertical micro-programming respectively?
questions.solution: Horizontal micro-programming has one bit per signal, so many signals can be activated simultaneously. Vertical micro-programming encodes the signals, so only one signal can be generated at a time. Answer: (32, 1).

questions.title: Control Unit Speed
questions.question: Vertical micro-programming, horizontal micro-programming and hardwired control are used for control unit design. Which of the following is correct about the highest and lowest operational speed respectively?
questions.solution: Hardwired control is the fastest (no control memory access). Vertical micro-programming is the slowest because of the extra decoding step, and horizontal is faster than vertical. So (a) and (c) are correct.

questions.title: Address Bus Size
questions.question: Consider a processor that can support a maximum memory of 8 GB, where the memory is word-addressable (a word consists of 2 bytes). The size of the address bus of the processor is at least:
questions.solution: 8 GB = 2^33 bytes. Number of words = 2^33 / 2 = 2^32, so 32 address bits.

questions.title: Tag Bits in Direct Mapped Cache
questions.question: Assume a direct mapped cache having 8 cache lines, each cache line consists of 2 words and each word is one byte. The address bus consists of 7 bits. The tag field of the cache consists of ___ bits.
questions.solution: Offset = log2(2) = 1 bit, line number = log2(8) = 3 bits. Tag = 7 − 3 − 1 = 3 bits.

questions.title: Tag Bits in 4-way Set Associative Cache
questions.question: Assume a 32-bit addressable physical memory and a 2 MB cache with block size 8 kB. How many bits are required in the tag field if the cache is 4-way set associative?
questions.solution: Block offset = log2(8K) = 13 bits. Number of blocks = 2MB / 8KB = 256, sets = 256 / 4 = 64, so index = 6 bits. Tag = 32 − 6 − 13 = 13 bits.

questions.title: Blocks and Tag Bits
questions.question: Consider a 16-KB cache where each block holds 32 bytes of data, the cache is 2-way set associative, physical addresses are 32 bits and the data is word addressed with 32-bit words. How many blocks are in this cache and how many tag bits are stored with each block entry?
questions.solution: Blocks = 16KB / 32B = 512. Sets = 512 / 2 = 256, so index = 8 bits. Block offset = 5 bits. Tag = 32 − 8 − 5 = 19 bits.

questions.title: Index Bits: Set vs Fully Associative
questions.question: Consider a 16 KB, two-way associative cache with 32-byte cache lines and a 64-bit address space. There will be p bits used for the index. If the same cache were fully associative, q bits would be used for the index. What is p + q?
questions.solution: Blocks = 512, sets = 256, so p = 8. A fully associative cache has only one set, so q = 0. p + q = 8.

questions.title: Number of Cache Lines
questions.question: Consider a system having a 512 KB, 16-way set associative L2 cache with a 128-byte cache line size. How many cache lines are present?

questions.title: Associativity from Tag Size
questions.question: Assume a cache with a 32-bit address, 768 blocks and a block size of 128 bytes. Tags are 17 bits. What is the associativity of the cache?
questions.solution: Offset = 7 bits, tag = 17 bits, so index = 32 − 17 − 7 = 8 bits = 256 sets. Associativity = 768 / 256 = 3-way.

questions.title: Direct Mapped Cache Contents
questions.question: Assume a direct mapped cache with 16 cache blocks (0–15) and a main memory having 256 blocks (0 to 255). Initially the cache is empty. Consider the memory block reference sequence: 3, 180, 43, 2, 191, 881, 190, 14, 181, 44, 186, 253. Which memory blocks are present in the cache after the sequence? (Note: 881 appears as typed in the source; it is likely 88, which gives the same cache line mapping in option (c).)

questions.title: Probability of Hit on Direct Mapped Cache
questions.question: Assume the access pattern x, y, z, y, x where each letter is a unique cache block, no block was accessed before, and all conflicts are random. What is the probability (closest to) of the second access to x being a hit on a direct mapped cache with 4 lines?
questions.solution: x stays in the cache only if neither y nor z maps to x's line. Each maps to a different line with probability 3/4, so P = (3/4)² = 56.25%, closest to 50%.

questions.title: Fastest Mapping Function
questions.question: Which one is the fastest cache mapping function among the following?
questions.solution: Direct mapping needs no search; each block maps to exactly one line, so the comparison is a single tag check. It is the fastest.

questions.title: Effective Access Time (Hierarchical)
questions.question: Suppose a cache has a 70% hit ratio, an access time of 50 ns on a cache hit and an access time of 120 ns on a cache miss. What is the effective access time (hierarchical memory)?
questions.solution: In hierarchical access, a miss costs cache time + memory time. EAT = 0.7 × 50 + 0.3 × (50 + 120) = 35 + 51 = 86 ns.

questions.title: Average Memory Access Time (Two Level)
questions.question: Suppose the local hit rate for L1 cache is 20% and the local hit rate for L2 cache is 30%. The hit time for L1 is 8 cycles, for L2 is 20 cycles and the access time for main memory is 30 cycles. What is the average memory access time in cycles (approximately)?

questions.title: Cache Statements
questions.question: Choose the correct statements from the following.
options: Instructions and data stored in cache are regularly used by the CPU; if data is not present in cache then it is always transferred from main memory.
Data is stored on a temporary basis in cache memory.
Programs stored in cache take more time to execute.
questions.solution: Cache holds frequently used data temporarily, has limited capacity, and misses are served from main memory. Programs in cache execute faster, not slower, so (c) is false.

questions.title: Compulsory and Conflict Misses
questions.question: Consider the following statements. S1: If the block size is increased then compulsory misses can be reduced. S2: If the associativity of the cache is increased then conflict misses can increase.
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true
questions.solution: A larger block brings more neighbouring data (spatial locality), reducing compulsory misses, so S1 is true. Higher associativity reduces conflict misses, so S2 is false.

questions.title: Average Time with Write Back
questions.question: Consider a 128-word cache and a main memory divided into 32-word blocks. Main memory access time is 50 µs/word and cache access time is 20 µs/word. The hit ratio for read operations is 80% and for write operations is 90%. On a cache miss, the associated block must be brought from main memory to cache for both read and write. 40% of references are writes. If the write-back policy is used and at any point of time 80% of cache blocks are modified, what is T_avg (up to 1 decimal, in µs)?

questions.title: Memory Size from Address Bits
questions.question: A 16-way set associative cache of size 128 KB is used in a system with a 32-bit address. For such a cache memory, the memory size is ___ (in Kbytes), given the block size is 4 bytes.
questions.solution: Main memory size is determined by the address bus: 2^32 bytes = 2^22 KB = 4194304 KB. Cache size, associativity and block size do not change the memory size.

questions.title: Decode IEEE 754 Number
questions.question: Consider the following IEEE single precision floating point number: 0100 0011 1101 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000. The decimal equivalent of the above number is ___

questions.title: Hex to Decimal (0x43758000)
questions.question: Consider the hexadecimal representation in IEEE 754 single precision: 0x43758000. What is the decimal value represented by it?

questions.title: Special Value
questions.question: In IEEE 754 single precision floating point, the number 1 11111111 000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 represents:
questions.solution: Sign = 1, exponent = all 1s (255) and mantissa = 0 represents −∞. A non-zero mantissa would be NaN.

questions.title: Hex to Decimal (0xC4127000)
questions.question: Consider the hexadecimal value 0xC4127000 in IEEE 754 single precision. What is the value represented in decimal?

questions.title: IEEE 754 Representation of 16
questions.question: What is the IEEE 754 32-bit floating point representation of 16?
questions.solution: 16 = 1.0 × 2^4. Exponent = 4 + 127 = 131 = 10000011, sign = 0, mantissa = 0, giving 0 10000011 000...0 (0x41800000). Option (c) is the closest match; the spacing of the digits in the source options looks garbled, so verify against your original sheet.

questions.title: Binary to Decimal
questions.question: Consider the binary value 0 10000111 1111010 0000 0000 0000 0000 in IEEE 754 single precision. What decimal value does it represent?

questions.title: Address Pins Saved
questions.question: Consider a 64-bit hypothetical CPU which supports a 256 KB memory space. The processor is enhanced with word-addressable memory. How many address pins are saved in the enhanced CPU to refer to the memory?
questions.solution: Byte addressable: 256 KB = 2^18 bytes → 18 pins. Word addressable (64-bit word = 8 bytes): 2^18 / 8 = 2^15 words → 15 pins. Pins saved = 18 − 15 = 3.

questions.title: RAM Chips Required
questions.question: How many 128 × 8 bit RAMs are required to design a 32K × 32 bit RAM?

questions.title: Program Counter Value
questions.question: Consider a 32-bit hypothetical CPU which supports word-addressable memory used to execute the following code. The code starting address is 2000. I1: 16 bytes, I2: 12 bytes, I3: 16 bytes, I4: 12 bytes, I5: 8 bytes, I6: 8 bytes. During the execution of I4, what would be the value in the program counter (PC)?
questions.solution: Word = 4 bytes, so sizes in words are 4, 3, 4, 3, 2, 2. Addresses: I1 = 2000, I2 = 2004, I3 = 2007, I4 = 2011, I5 = 2014. During execution of I4 the PC already points to the next instruction, I5 = 2014.

questions.title: Match the Registers
questions.question: Match Column I with Column II. Column I: A. Program counter (PC), B. Memory Address Register (MAR), C. Instruction Register (IR), D. Accumulator (AC). Column II: (i) Contains the instruction currently being executed by the CPU, (ii) Contains the temporary result or first operand of an ALU operation, (iii) Contains the starting address of the next instruction to be fetched, (iv) Contains the address of the memory location used for a read or write operation.
questions.solution: PC → next instruction address (iii), MAR → memory location address (iv), IR → current instruction (i), AC → temporary result / first operand (ii).

questions.title: 8085 Program
questions.question: What does the following program produce when run on an 8085 microprocessor? LDA 8000H; MVI B, 30H; ADD B; STA 8001H
options: Read a number from an input port and store it in memory.
Read a number from an input device with address 8000H and store it in memory.
Read a number from memory location 8000H and store it in memory location 8001H.
questions.solution: The program loads the byte at memory 8000H into A, adds 30H (from B), and stores the result at 8001H. Since 30H is added before storing, it is not a plain copy, so none of the options (a)–(c) is correct.

questions.title: Program Counter (Byte Addressable)
questions.question: Consider a 64-bit hypothetical CPU which supports byte-addressable memory used to execute the following code. The code starting address is 1000. I1: 2 bytes, I2: 4 bytes, I3: 4 bytes, I4: 4 bytes, I5: 2 bytes, I6: 6 bytes. During the execution of I5, what would be the value in the program counter (PC)?
questions.solution: Addresses: I1 = 1000, I2 = 1002, I3 = 1006, I4 = 1010, I5 = 1014, I6 = 1016. During execution of I5 the PC holds the address of I6 = 1016.

questions.title: Memory Accesses over 8-bit Bus
questions.question: To execute a program, instructions have to be brought from memory to the CPU using a bus. If the bus has 8 lines, at most one byte (8 bits) can be transferred at a time. How many memory accesses are required to transfer a 32-bit instruction from memory to the CPU?
questions.solution: 32 bits / 8 bits per transfer = 4 memory accesses.

questions.title: Endianness
questions.question: Consider the statements. S1: In little endian, the lower address contains the lower byte and the higher address contains the higher byte. S2: In big endian, the lower address contains the higher byte and the higher address contains the lower byte.
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true
questions.solution: Little endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address; big endian stores the most significant byte at the lowest address. Both statements are true.

questions.title: Accumulator and PC Statements
questions.question: Consider the statements. S1: The accumulator stores the results of calculations made by the ALU. S2: The program counter keeps track of the memory location of the current instruction that the processor is currently dealing with.
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true
questions.solution: S1 is true. S2 is false: the PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched, not the current one.

questions.title: CPU Register Statements
questions.question: Which of the statements is/are true?
options: Memory address register stores the memory locations in the instruction that need to be fetched from memory.
Memory data register stores the instruction fetched from memory or any data that is to be transferred to and stored in memory.
Instruction register stores the most recently fetched instruction.
Instruction buffer register contains the instructions which are not to be executed immediately.
questions.solution: All four statements correctly describe MAR, MDR, IR and IBR.

questions.title: Primitive Instruction
questions.question: Which of the following is a primitive instruction in the CPU?
options: opcode (4 bits), Address-1 (4 bits), Address-2 (4 bits)
opcode (2 bits), Address-1 (12 bits), Address-2 (8 bits)
questions.solution: A primitive (regular) instruction format has equal-sized address fields, as in the 4-bit opcode with two 4-bit addresses. Treat this as low confidence and verify against your answer key, since the term is not defined in the source.

questions.title: Maximum Number of Instructions
questions.question: Consider a hypothetical system which supports only 2-address instructions. If the instruction size is 28 bits and the size of each address is 10 bits, the maximum number of instructions the system can support is ___
questions.solution: Opcode = 28 − 2 × 10 = 8 bits, so 2^8 = 256 instructions.

questions.title: Instruction Size in Bytes
questions.question: Consider a digital computer which supports 64 three-address instructions. If the size of each address is 14 bits, the instruction is of ___ bytes.
questions.solution: Opcode = log2(64) = 6 bits. Instruction = 6 + 3 × 14 = 48 bits = 6 bytes.

questions.title: Fetch-Execute Cycle
questions.question: The correct sequence in the Fetch-Execute cycle is:
questions.solution: The instruction is first fetched, then decoded, then executed.

questions.title: Instruction Size Formula
questions.question: Consider a system which supports 2-address instructions only. The system has 2^p K bytes of memory. If there are q distinct instructions supported by the system, what is the size of the instruction?
questions.solution: Memory = 2^p × 2^10 bytes, so each address is (p + 10) bits. Opcode = log q bits. Instruction = log q + 2(p + 10) bits.

questions.title: Expanding Opcode (1-address)
questions.question: Consider a system which supports both 2-address and 1-address instructions. The system has 6-bit instructions and 2-bit addresses. If there are three 2-address instructions in the system, what is the maximum and minimum number of 1-address instructions the system can support?
questions.solution: 2-address opcode = 6 − 4 = 2 bits, giving 4 opcodes, of which 3 are used. The 1 free opcode is expanded using the 2-bit address field: 2^2 = 4 one-address instructions (maximum). Since the system supports 1-address instructions, the minimum is 1.

questions.title: PC-Relative Branch
questions.question: Consider a PC-relative mode branch instruction which branches to address 680 in memory. The instruction has an offset value of 420. What is the address of this instruction in memory, if each instruction is stored in 2 memory locations?
questions.solution: Target = PC + offset, so PC = 680 − 420 = 260. The PC points to the next instruction, so the branch instruction is at 260 − 2 = 258.

questions.title: Fetch vs Execute Time
questions.question: Consider a 6-word instruction of the type: opcode, Mode-1, Mode-2, Address-1, Address-2. The first operand (destination) uses register indirect mode and the second operand uses indirect mode. Each operand is 2 words, each address is 2 words and main memory takes 20 ns per word access. What is the difference between the instruction fetch time and the execution time? (Register access time is negligible.)
questions.solution: Fetch = 6 words × 20 = 120 ns. Execution: source (indirect) = pointer 2 words (40) + operand 2 words (40) = 80 ns; destination (register indirect) read 40 ns and write-back 40 ns, so execution = 160 ns. Difference = 160 − 120 = 40 ns.

questions.title: Zero-Address Instructions
questions.question: Consider a computer with 34-bit instructions and 14-bit addresses. If there are 60 two-address instructions and 65000 one-address instructions, how many zero-address instructions can be formulated at most?
questions.solution: 2-address opcode = 34 − 28 = 6 bits → 64 codes, 4 free. 1-address: 4 × 2^14 = 65536 codes, 65000 used → 536 free. 0-address: 536 × 2^14 = 8,781,824 = 8576 K.

questions.title: Opcode Instruction Types
questions.question: If an opcode is 4 bits, what is the maximum and minimum number of types of instructions supported by the CPU?
questions.solution: A 4-bit opcode gives 2^4 = 16 distinct codes (maximum). A CPU must support at least 1 instruction, so the minimum is 1.

questions.title: Functions of I/O Module
questions.question: Which of the following is/are not the major functions of an I/O module?
questions.solution: Control and timing, processor communication, device communication, data buffering and error detection are I/O module functions. SIMD is a parallel processing classification, not an I/O function.

questions.title: Interrupt vs Programmed I/O Gain
questions.question: Consider a system with a data transfer rate of 10 KBPS. Data is exchanged between the processor and the I/O interface. Find the performance gain when the I/O device operates under interrupt mode over programmed I/O mode. (Interrupt interface overhead is 15 µsec; round off to 1 decimal place.)
questions.solution: Time per byte = 1 / 10 KBPS = 100 µs. In programmed I/O the CPU is busy for the whole 100 µs. In interrupt mode the CPU is busy only for the 15 µs overhead. Gain = 100 / 15 ≈ 6.7.

questions.title: Programmed I/O Transfer Time
questions.question: In programmed I/O execution, the transfer time depends on:
options: Latency of the I/O interface chip
questions.solution: Transfer time in programmed I/O depends on the speed of the I/O device, the amount of data to be transferred and the latency of the interface chip. Verify against your answer key as the source did not provide one.

questions.title: Speedup of Programmed I/O over Interrupt Mode
questions.question: Consider the following scenario: data transfer rate is 10 KBPS and the interrupt interface overhead is 15 µsec (same scenario as the previous NAT question). Calculate the speedup when the I/O device is operating under programmed I/O over interrupt mode. (Round off to 2 decimal places.)
questions.solution: Time per byte = 100 µs. CPU time per byte: programmed I/O = 100 µs, interrupt mode = 15 µs. Speedup of programmed I/O over interrupt = 15 / 100 = 0.15 (i.e. programmed I/O is actually slower; the inverse of the 6.7 gain in the previous question).

questions.title: Software Interrupts
questions.question: Interrupts which are caused by software instructions are known as:
questions.solution: Interrupts generated by software instructions or by errors during instruction execution (traps) are exception interrupts.

questions.title: DMA Cycles for File Transfer
questions.question: Consider a 16 MBPS I/O device interfaced to a 32-bit CPU using a DMA interface. The DMA contains a 16-bit count register, a 32-bit data register and five 8-bit address registers. The data file size is 512 kB. How many DMA cycles are required to transfer the file?
questions.solution: File = 512 KB / 4 B per word = 128 K = 2^17 words. The 16-bit count register can handle 2^16 transfers per DMA cycle (programming). Cycles = 2^17 / 2^16 = 2.

questions.title: Address Bus Size
questions.question: A processor can support a maximum memory of 32 GB, where the memory is word addressable (a word consists of 2 bytes). The size of the address bus of the processor is at least ___ bits.
questions.solution: 32 GB = 2^35 bytes. Words = 2^35 / 2 = 2^34, so 34 address bits.
